248.bp: A click-through-rate system decides which advertisement, product, or recommendation is likely to be clicked in the next moment. The useful evidence is often a person's history: searches, views, purchases, skips, and returns over a long period. Industrial recommender systems want to use much longer histories because old behavior can reveal durable taste, seasonal habits, and repeated cycles that a short window misses. The problem is that reading a long history naively is expensive. SparseCTR serves the practical need of making long-term user behavior usable in production click prediction. It asks how a model can remember enough of a user's past to predict the next click while avoiding the cost of comparing every past action with every other past action. The paper is not just trying to make a larger recommender. It is trying to make long-history modeling fit the time and cost limits of real advertising and recommendation systems.
248.wh: The hard part is that user behavior has both length and uneven meaning. Some actions reveal stable interests, such as a long-running preference for a category. Some actions mark a transition, such as moving from browsing phones to comparing accessories. Some actions are short-lived, such as a recent search that only matters today. Standard self-attention, meaning a mechanism that lets every past behavior compare itself with every other behavior to decide what matters, grows too costly as the sequence becomes long. The cost rises roughly with all pairs of past events, so adding more history can quickly become impractical. Sparse attention methods from other fields reduce comparisons, but the abstract says they do not fit recommendation directly because users differ from one another and their interests change over time. A fixed sparse pattern can cut away the wrong evidence: it may split a continuous activity, miss a user's personal rhythm, or ignore periodic behavior.
248.naive: A smart beginner would take a successful long-sequence model and feed it the full user history. Every behavior would be allowed to look at every other behavior, and the model would learn which older actions should influence the click prediction. This fails on cost first: long industrial histories make full pairwise comparison too slow and expensive to deploy. The next beginner move would be to keep only recent behavior or use a generic sparse pattern that checks selected positions. That saves work but fails on meaning. A recent-only window loses durable interests, and a generic pattern may break an uninterrupted shopping session into pieces or treat two users with different rhythms as if their histories should be cut and read the same way.
248.ap: SparseCTR's core idea is to make the history smaller in a way that respects how recommendations behave. First, it divides a user's behavior sequence into chunks personalized to that user, so a run of related actions is less likely to be split by an arbitrary boundary. Chunking also lets parts of the long sequence be processed in parallel, which saves time. Then, instead of using one sparse reading pattern, the model uses three branches. One branch looks for global interests, the broad preferences that remain useful across the long history. A second branch looks for interest transitions, the points where the user's direction changes. A third branch looks for short-term interests, the recent signal that may dominate the next click. The paper also adds relative temporal encoding, meaning learned bias terms that tell the model how order, distance, and periodic timing between behaviors should change their influence.
248.mech: The input is an ordered record of user behaviors and the prediction target is whether the next displayed item will be clicked. SparseCTR first segments the behavior sequence into chunks. The important detail is that the segmentation is personalized: the model is not merely cutting every user after the same number of events. It tries to avoid separating continuous behavior, because a burst of related actions often carries meaning as a unit. Once the sequence is chunked, the model can process pieces of the history in parallel instead of walking through the whole record as one slow chain. On top of those chunks, the three sparse self-attention branches read different kinds of evidence. The global branch asks which parts of the long record express broad interests. The transition branch asks where the user appears to be moving from one interest state to another. The short-term branch gives more direct influence to recent behavior. Each branch performs selective comparison rather than full all-to-all comparison, so it spends computation on structured parts of the history. The temporal encoding then adds information about relative order and timing. Its learnable, head-specific bias coefficients let different comparison heads assign different importance to recency, sequence distance, and periodic patterns. The outputs of these branches become a user-behavior representation used to score click likelihood.
248.math: The main mathematical idea is selective weighted comparison over an ordered sequence. Each behavior is an event in time, and the system must decide how strongly one event should influence the reading of another. Full attention gives the model a possible weight for every pair of events, which is expressive but costly. Sparse attention restricts which pairs are considered, turning the problem from checking everything into checking a carefully chosen subset. This is a tradeoff between completeness and cost: fewer comparisons save time, but the sparse pattern must preserve the comparisons that carry click-prediction signal. Chunking is a form of structured compression. It groups nearby or continuous actions so the model handles larger meaningful units instead of isolated clicks. The three branches express a decomposition of behavior into time scales: long-term preference, change between preferences, and immediate intent. Relative temporal encoding adds another mathematical object: a learned bias based on the distance or relation between event times. A bias is a small push in the score before the final weighting is chosen. Head-specific coefficients mean different readers inside the model can learn different timing rules. This fits recommendation because time is not only order; spacing and repetition change what a past action means.
248.dots: This paper sits where recommendation, sequence modeling, ranking, and attention meet. Like other recommendation papers, it must rank or score candidate items under limited user attention, and the top few scores matter most because those are what the system will show. Like sequence papers, it treats behavior as an ordered path rather than a bag of clicks; the same product view can mean something different if it follows a long search session or appears months after a purchase. Like attention papers, it asks which pieces of evidence should speak loudly and which should mostly stay quiet. Its neighboring family includes dynamic recommendation work that tries to preserve chronological context and generative recommendation work that tries to avoid noisy attention over sparse histories. SparseCTR's distinctive pressure is industrial scale: it wants long histories and larger computation budgets to keep helping, but only if the comparison pattern remains cheap enough to deploy.
248.ww: The mechanism should improve over the naive choices because it matches the shape of user behavior more closely. Full self-attention wastes work by allowing every old action to inspect every other old action, even though most pairs are unlikely to matter for the next click. A recent-only shortcut saves work but throws away stable preferences and recurring patterns. SparseCTR tries to keep the middle ground: it spends comparison work on global interests, transitions, and short-term behavior because those are the three kinds of evidence the abstract identifies as important. Personalized chunks help because user histories do not arrive in neat fixed-size blocks. One user may make many related actions in a short burst; another may spread a similar decision across time. Cutting both histories by the same ruler can destroy the continuity that explains intent. The temporal bias helps because two behaviors with the same item labels can carry different meaning depending on their distance, order, and periodic relation. If these structures repeat across many users, learning them should produce better click scores with less unnecessary computation.
248.po: The reported payoff is twofold: SparseCTR is more efficient and more effective for long-term behavior CTR prediction. The abstract says it outperforms prior methods, shows a clear scaling-law phenomenon across three orders of magnitude in FLOPs, and remains useful as more computation is spent. It also reports online A/B test gains of 1.72 percent in CTR and 1.41 percent in CPM. In practical terms, the system buys a way to use longer user histories in deployed recommendation and advertising settings without paying the full cost of all-pairs attention.
248.limits: The claims depend on user histories having learnable structure at the levels SparseCTR models: global interests, transitions, short-term intent, and temporal or periodic relations. If behavior is sparse, noisy, manipulated, or driven by events not visible in the logs, the learned sparse pattern may focus on the wrong evidence. The abstract does not specify the exact chunking rule, how sensitive results are to each branch, or where the method becomes too expensive. It reports strong experiments and online lifts, but the abstract alone does not prove the same gains for every platform, item domain, privacy setting, cold-start user, or rapidly changing recommendation environment.

249.bp: Many allocation systems are not just handing out objects to people. They are assigning work into roles. A research project, a support duty, or an administrative chore may be easy or painful depending on the position where it lands, because each position comes with different tools, authority, support, and background expectations. The paper starts from that ordinary mismatch. Traditional allocation models usually say that an agent has one fixed value or cost for an item, no matter where the item is consumed. This paper asks what happens when the same item changes value with the assigned position, and when some assignments are forbidden. In the graph version, positions are points and items are links between positions; each item must be sent to one of the positions it touches. The goal is to make an assignment that is fair to agents while also avoiding wasteful arrangements.
249.wh: The difficulty comes from three pressures arriving at once. First, value depends on position, so the system cannot write one simple preference list for each agent and reuse it everywhere. Second, feasibility is constrained: a task cannot always go to every position, just as the abstract says a research project cannot be assigned to administrative staff. Third, fairness and efficiency can pull against each other. A fair-looking assignment may waste total effort, while the most efficient assignment may load the best-supported positions or agents in a way that feels unacceptable. The graph constraint makes this sharper because each item has only a small local choice, one endpoint or the other. A decision made for one edge changes what remains possible around nearby vertices. The system therefore has to reason about a whole arrangement, not independent task choices, while still measuring each agent's fair share and the collective quality of the outcome.
249.naive: A smart beginner might first ignore positions and give each item to the agent who values it most, or who can complete the chore with the least effort. That fails because the value is not attached to the item alone; it is attached to the item together with the position. The same agent may face different resources and support at different positions. Another beginner move is to respect eligibility rules first, then fix unfairness afterward. But once each graph edge has been oriented to one endpoint, later repairs can be blocked by the same eligibility rules. Moving one task to help one agent may be impossible, or may break efficiency elsewhere. The hard part is choosing feasible, fair, and efficient assignments together.
249.ap: The paper's central move is to model the allocation as a position-aware graph assignment. Positions become vertices. Items become edges. Assigning an item means choosing which endpoint receives that edge, which is why the abstract connects the setting to the orientation problem. On top of that graph skeleton, agents have values that depend on the position they receive, not only on the item. The paper then studies which guarantees can be achieved when fairness is measured by maximin share, meaning the level an agent could secure in a cautious divide-and-choose thought experiment, and when efficiency is measured by Pareto optimality and social optimality. Pareto optimality asks whether any agent can be helped without hurting another; social optimality asks about the total value or cost of the assignment. The contribution is a map of computational difficulty plus approximation algorithms when exact efficient and fair allocation is too demanding.
249.mech: The mechanism begins with three inputs: a set of agents, a set of positions, and a set of items whose allowable positions are restricted. In the graph case, each item is represented as an edge joining exactly the positions that may receive it. The algorithmic task is to orient every edge toward one incident vertex, which means deciding the position where that item will be allocated. For each possible decision, the system must look up how the relevant agent values that item at that position. It cannot replace this with a single item value, because the paper's setting is precisely that position changes the effort, resources, or benefit attached to the item. Once a tentative orientation is made, each agent's bundle can be evaluated. Fairness is checked against maximin share: what the agent could reasonably expect if the items were partitioned under a worst-case choice rule. Efficiency is checked in two ways. Pareto optimality rejects an assignment if another feasible orientation would improve someone without making anyone else worse off. Social optimality compares the total value or total burden across assignments. The paper's results then separate cases where such assignments can be computed exactly from cases where approximation algorithms are needed, meaning algorithms that promise a controlled closeness to the desired fairness or efficiency target.
249.math: The main mathematical object is a graph used as a map of permission. Vertices are positions, edges are items, and orienting an edge is the act of choosing which allowed position receives the item. This is graph reasoning in a concrete sense: links do not merely show similarity; they state a hard local choice. The second object is a valuation table that depends on both item and position. That table is the reason ordinary allocation math is not enough, because a value is not a property of the item alone. The fairness idea is maximin share. In plain terms, it asks what level an agent could protect for herself if she had to divide the work into bundles while someone else chose the bundle for her. It is a cautious fairness yardstick, useful when exact equality is impossible. The efficiency ideas define what counts as waste. Pareto optimality says an assignment is wasteful if another feasible assignment helps at least one agent and harms none. Social optimality adds up value or cost and asks for the best collective total. The algorithmic part is computational complexity and approximation: proving when the search over graph orientations is easy, when it is inherently hard, and when a guaranteed near-answer is the right mathematical compromise.
249.dots: This paper connects to several recurring conference ideas without looking like a prediction or ranking paper. It is a matching problem because tasks must be paired with allowed positions under scarcity and preferences. It is a graph problem because the allowed choices are encoded by edges and vertices, so local eligibility shapes the global solution. It is also an optimization problem in the plain sense: define what counts as unfair or wasteful, then search over feasible assignments that reduce those failures. Within the fair allocation theme, it sits next to chore-allocation work that uses maximin share to stop one participant from being overburdened, and next to efficiency papers that ask which guarantees survive when exact solutions are computationally expensive. Its distinctive surface is position-aware valuation. The deeper shared issue is that a fair decision is rarely just choosing the best item for each person; it is choosing a whole feasible arrangement under rules, scarcity, and competing notions of value.
249.ww: The approach can improve over the naive one because it keeps the real source of difficulty inside the model instead of smoothing it away. If position changes the available support, then a value attached only to an item is a false shortcut. By using position-aware valuations, the method can distinguish a task that is easy in one role from the same task becoming costly in another. If eligibility constraints form a graph, then graph orientation gives the algorithm a direct language for the actual decision: each constrained item must be pushed to one of its allowed endpoints. Fairness and efficiency are also checked at the assignment level, which matters because unfairness can be created by the pile as a whole even when every single local choice looks reasonable. Maximin share gives a cautious baseline for what each agent should be able to expect, while Pareto and social optimality prevent the fairness target from hiding needless waste. The complete complexity and approximation results matter because they tell designers when this richer model is still computable and when they must accept a controlled relaxation.
249.po: The payoff is a clearer theory for allocation systems where context changes value. The paper does not merely add another fairness label; it studies a more realistic setting in which positions carry different resources and support, items may be eligible for only certain positions, and the graph orientation view captures those restrictions. Its stated result is a complete set of computational complexity and approximation results for computing allocations that are efficient and fair. That gives a designer two kinds of guidance: which versions of the problem can be solved directly, and which require algorithms that trade exactness for a provable guarantee.
249.limits: The abstract describes a theoretical model, so its claims depend on the valuations and constraints being known accurately. If agents misstate how costly a chore is at a position, or if support and resources change after assignment, the computed fairness may not match lived fairness. The graph case also assumes each item is naturally tied to incident positions; some real tasks may have richer eligibility rules than a simple edge can express. The abstract promises complexity and approximation results, but it does not state empirical deployment, strategic behavior, dynamic arrivals of tasks, or how valuations are elicited. The guarantees are therefore strongest for settings that fit the model cleanly.

250.bp: The paper is about a very practical edge-device problem: small machines are being asked to understand many kinds of sensor signals without sending everything to a cloud server. An Internet of Things camera, wearable, phone, or embedded controller may need to recognize events locally, but it has little memory and that memory can change as other processes run. Spiking neural networks are attractive here because they process events over time: instead of doing the same heavy calculation for every input position, they react when spike-like signals appear. That can save energy, which matters on devices with tight batteries. MASI asks what has to happen after such a model is already chosen and must actually run on hardware. The real object is not only the model. It is the live memory budget around the model: how much space is free now, how much the next layer needs, how many timesteps are still useful, and how to finish the prediction without falling off the device's limits.
250.wh: The hard part is that spiking neural networks are efficient in one sense but awkward in another. They do not simply pass an input through a fixed stack once. They evolve across timesteps, keeping temporary activity from one moment to the next. That means memory pressure depends on both the model layers and the time dimension. A device may have enough memory for one moment, then lose some to another task, then recover some later. A simple memory plan made before inference can become wrong while the model is running. Prior lightweight model design attacks the problem by making the model smaller, but the abstract says that can sacrifice accuracy. System-level memory management tries to move memory around during execution, but timestep-dependent dynamics can make that management expensive at runtime. MASI is hard because it must solve three goals together: fit into fluctuating memory, avoid wasting memory in fragments, and cut redundant timestep work without noticeably hurting the answer.
250.naive: A smart beginner would first shrink the spiking model until it fits the smallest expected memory budget. That is safe but blunt: the device may often have more memory available, and the smaller model may lose accuracy because useful layers or internal detail were removed. Another beginner would keep the model unchanged and rely on ordinary memory management to load and unload pieces as needed. That also breaks because spiking inference changes across timesteps; managing every timestep separately can add overhead large enough to erase the efficiency benefit. A third beginner would run all timesteps every time, assuming more computation is safer. MASI is built around the observation that these choices waste either accuracy, time, memory, or all three.
250.ap: MASI's central move is to make inference adapt to the device while the prediction is being produced. It does this with three cooperating parts. First, it slices layers into finer pieces so the system can choose a piece size that fits the memory currently available rather than treating each full layer as an all-or-nothing block. Second, it schedules those pieces in a way that does not depend on a detailed timestep plan. The scheduler tries to pack work into available memory and reduce fragmentation, meaning small unusable gaps that leave memory technically free but practically unhelpful. Third, it watches the time evolution of the spiking network and exits early when later timesteps are likely to repeat work that no longer changes the result much. The core idea is therefore not simply compression. It is a runtime controller that decides how much of the model to hold, when to run it, and when enough evidence has accumulated.
250.mech: The input is an on-device spiking neural network, a stream or representation of sensed data, and a memory situation that may be strict and may change during runtime. MASI first treats the network as a sequence of layers whose intermediate results must be held only long enough to continue the calculation. Instead of requiring a whole layer to fit as one unit, the fine-grained slicing strategy divides layer work into smaller memory-adaptive units. If less memory is available, the slices can be smaller; if more memory is available, larger or more efficient groupings can be used. The scheduler then decides how to place these slices into the current memory budget. Its goal is high memory utilization with little fragmentation, so the available space is used as a workable workspace rather than becoming a pile of scattered gaps. The abstract calls this scheduler timestep-agnostic because it avoids making the whole memory plan depend on the detailed behavior of each timestep. During inference, the network still advances through timesteps, accumulating spike-driven evidence for an output. MASI's early-exit part observes that not every input needs all planned timesteps. When the prediction has become stable enough, it stops further timestep calculations and returns the result. The output is the same kind of inference result the spiking model would produce, but reached under a memory plan that adapts to runtime availability and avoids redundant late computation.
250.math: The mathematical center is resource-constrained scheduling and early stopping. Scheduling means deciding which pieces of work occupy which pieces of memory at which moments. The scarce object is memory, and the score being improved is not only accuracy but usable packing: high memory utilization, low fragmentation, and low latency. Fragmentation is a geometric idea in a small workspace. Ten units of free memory are not equally useful if they are split into many tiny holes; a computation may need one continuous enough region to run efficiently. Layer slicing turns a coarse packing problem into a finer one by changing the size of the blocks being placed. That creates flexibility but also more scheduling decisions. The timestep-agnostic part is a simplification of the decision space: the scheduler should not have to rebuild a complex plan for every time step of the spiking dynamics. The other mathematical idea is sequential decision making with a stopping rule. Each timestep adds more evidence, but later evidence may have shrinking value. Early exit asks when the expected gain from one more timestep is smaller than the cost in time and memory. The tradeoff is accuracy versus resource use. MASI works only if the stopping signal identifies cases where extra timesteps are mostly redundant.
250.dots: Within the repo's current map, MASI sits in the neuromorphic edge computing theme and also connects to the broader efficiency and optimization thread. Its sibling idea is SpikeQuant, another spiking-neural-network paper in the JSON data, but the two attack different parts of the edge problem. SpikeQuant changes how large-model values are represented and computed so arithmetic becomes cheaper. MASI instead assumes an on-device spiking model must be scheduled under changing memory limits. Both reflect the same pressure: edge devices need useful local inference while saving memory, energy, or time. MASI also sits near systems papers that optimize under physical limits, such as latency, communication, capacity, or device resources. The recurring conference idea is choosing a workable point under constraints. Unlike ranking papers that sort documents or recommendation papers that sort items, MASI ranks and schedules pieces of computation. Unlike privacy papers, it does not primarily hide data, although local edge inference can reduce reliance on cloud execution. Its main connection is systems math: budgeting scarce memory and time while preserving enough predictive evidence.
250.ww: MASI should improve over the naive approaches because it attacks wasted resources at the level where the waste appears. Shrinking the model permanently assumes the worst memory case all the time. MASI instead adapts to the current memory case, so it can use more of the device when more is available and still survive when less is available. Ordinary memory management can waste time because spiking networks unfold across timesteps; MASI reduces that overhead by making the scheduler less dependent on timestep-specific plans. Layer slicing helps because a layer that is too large as one block may become runnable when divided into smaller pieces. Better packing helps because free memory only matters if computation can actually use it. Early exit helps for a different reason: spiking inference often accumulates evidence over time, and once the output has effectively settled, later timesteps may repeat the same conclusion at real cost. The abstract's reported combination, lower memory use and much lower latency with negligible accuracy loss, is exactly what one would expect if the three parts remove different forms of waste rather than all sacrificing the same model capacity.
250.po: The payoff is a more practical path for running spiking neural networks on mobile and embedded devices. MASI dynamically adapts to runtime memory availability instead of requiring a fixed memory assumption. In the abstract's evaluation across diverse workloads and edge devices, it reduces memory usage by about 20.67 percent and inference latency by 58.53 percent on average compared with other feasible on-device implementations under memory constraints. The claimed accuracy loss is negligible. In ordinary terms, the paper buys local sensing inference that is less likely to fail when memory is tight and less likely to waste time when the network has already gathered enough evidence.
250.limits: The abstract leaves several assumptions open. MASI depends on spiking-network computations being sliceable in a way that does not create too much extra overhead or destroy the model's accuracy. It also depends on memory availability being observable quickly enough for runtime adaptation to help. Early exit assumes later timesteps are sometimes redundant and that the system can detect that safely; if a task needs late-arriving spikes to distinguish hard cases, stopping early could be risky. The abstract reports diverse workloads and devices, but it does not specify which memory patterns, model sizes, or sensing modalities are hardest. It also compares with feasible on-device implementations under memory constraints, not every possible hardware-specific hand-tuned implementation.

251.bp: This paper is about choosing which columns of a dataset are worth keeping when the data comes from several places. Imagine several hospitals, markets, classrooms, or websites that all record the same kinds of measurements, but each place has different people or events. The task is not to predict a known label, because the setting is unsupervised: the method must judge useful features without being told the correct answer for each sample. The practical need is simple. If a later model keeps noisy or misleading features, it may learn patterns that belong only to one source and fail elsewhere. The paper focuses on multi-source feature selection, where the sources share a feature space but not the same samples. Its main concern is that a feature can look important merely because of source bias or a hidden common cause. UMCFS tries to select features that reflect stable underlying structure across sources, not accidental correlations inside one source.
251.wh: The hard part is that the same feature can mean different things across sources, even when every source uses the same column name. One source may contain older users, another may contain different products, and another may have a different measuring process. A feature can therefore appear strongly tied to the rest of the data in one source because of who happened to be sampled, not because the feature carries a stable signal. Single-source unsupervised feature selection is already difficult because there are no labels saying which features matter. In the multi-source case, the method must also decide which patterns are shared and which are local quirks. Correlation makes this worse. Two features can move together because one causes the other, because both are shaped by a third hidden factor, or because a source has a biased mixture of samples. Treating all co-movement as importance risks selecting features that do not travel across sources.
251.naive: A smart beginner might put all sources into one table and run a standard unsupervised feature selector. That would rank features by how much they preserve visible structure, such as groups of similar samples or strong relationships among columns. Another beginner might run feature selection separately in each source and average the rankings. Both ideas miss the same issue: they treat observed association as trustworthy. Pooling lets large or unusual sources dominate the decision. Separating sources makes it hard to tell whether a feature is globally useful or merely useful in one place. Neither approach asks whether a hidden factor has made an irrelevant feature look important. So the chosen feature set may fit the collected sources while failing on a new source.
251.ap: The paper's central move is to make feature selection act less like simple popularity counting and more like a careful comparison across sources. UMCFS first learns sample weights that balance the sources. A weight is a way of saying that some samples should count more and others less so the combined data is not tilted toward source-specific accidents. The abstract says this is done with adversarial balancing: the method tries to make weighted samples less revealing of which source they came from. Once the sources are better balanced, the method performs causal reweighting, meaning it uses the weights to reduce relationships that are likely caused by hidden bias rather than stable influence. It then separates two kinds of feature importance: a shared global part that should hold across sources, and source-specific deviations that are allowed to differ. The selected features are those whose importance survives this separation.
251.mech: The input is a collection of datasets from multiple sources. Each source has different samples, but every sample is described using the same feature columns. Because there are no labels, the method cannot ask which features predict a target. Instead, it must inspect the structure inside the measurements. First, UMCFS considers the source identity of each sample as a possible source of bias. It assigns sample weights so that, after weighting, the sources are less distinguishable from each other. The adversarial part can be understood as a contest: one side tries to choose weights that hide source identity in the weighted data, while the other side tries to detect the source. Better weights make source-specific imbalance less dominant. Second, the method uses these weights for causal reweighting, so feature relationships that were strong only because of uneven source composition are weakened. Third, it evaluates feature importance in two pieces. One piece is global: does this feature consistently help explain shared structure across sources? The other piece is local: how much does its apparent importance drift within a particular source? The output is a ranked or selected set of features that emphasizes shared importance while accounting for source-specific deviations.
251.math: The main mathematical idea is weighting as controlled re-counting. Ordinary counting treats every sample equally, but equal counting can be unfair to the question when sources have different mixtures of samples. A weight changes how much each sample contributes, so the combined dataset can imitate a more balanced comparison. The second idea is adversarial balancing, which is a two-player scoring problem. One score rewards weights that make samples from different sources look alike in the ways relevant to feature selection; an opposing score checks whether source identity can still be recovered. This is a form of optimization: define what counts as wrong, here source imbalance and misleading associations, then adjust controllable weights and importance scores to reduce that wrongness. The causal part is the distinction between moving together and one thing truly explaining another. If a hidden factor affects both a feature and the observed structure, correlation overstates the feature's value. Reweighting tries to compare samples more like with like, reducing confounding-induced spurious correlations. The final decomposition into global importance and source-specific deviation is also mathematical bookkeeping: split one score into a stable shared component and local residuals, then prefer the stable component.
251.dots: This paper sits in the causal-inference part of the conference because it asks whether an observed relationship should be trusted as a reason to keep a feature. It also touches domain adaptation, where models must work across different data sources rather than only where they were trained. The nearby idea in recommendation, search, and fairness papers is the same: raw historical data is not a neutral mirror of the world. It contains selection effects, popularity effects, source effects, and hidden causes. UMCFS applies that pressure to feature selection rather than ranking users or documents. It also connects to representation and graph papers that separate shared structure from local noise, but here the object being cleaned is the set of input columns. The family resemblance is the move from surface association to stable evidence: balance the comparison, discount source-specific artifacts, and keep the signal that repeats across environments.
251.ww: The method should improve over the naive approach if the most useful features are the ones whose importance remains visible after sources are balanced. Source bias can make a feature look valuable because the feature marks where the sample came from, not because it captures the underlying structure shared by all sources. By learning weights that reduce source identity, UMCFS makes it harder for this shortcut to dominate. Causal reweighting then changes the evidence used to judge each feature: instead of asking only whether the feature moves with other measurements, it asks whether that relationship persists under a more balanced view of the samples. The global-versus-local split adds another guardrail. A feature that is important everywhere is treated differently from one that spikes in a single source. That distinction matters because multi-source selection is meant to produce a feature set that can survive heterogeneity. The intuition is not that local deviations are useless, but that they should not be confused with shared importance.
251.po: The payoff is a feature-selection method for multi-source data that does not require labels and does not rely only on raw correlations. According to the abstract, UMCFS combines adversarial balancing, causal reweighting, and a separation between shared global importance and source-specific deviations. That buys a more reliable way to evaluate features when sources contain different samples but share the same columns. The claimed experimental result is that UMCFS consistently improves feature selection performance, though the provided abstract text is cut off before the full result details. In practical terms, the output is a smaller or better-ranked feature set that should be less tied to one source's quirks.
251.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The sources must share a meaningful feature space; if the same column has incompatible meaning across sources, balancing cannot fully repair that. The method also assumes that source differences provide useful evidence for separating shared importance from local deviation. If every source has the same hidden bias, cross-source comparison may not expose it. The abstract says the method works without label supervision, so its feature choices depend on unsupervised structure rather than direct task outcomes. It also does not, in the visible text, prove true causality in the experimental settings; it describes causal reweighting meant to mitigate confounding-induced spurious correlations. The full abstract is truncated, so exact datasets, metrics, and failure cases cannot be verified here.

252.bp: The ordinary problem behind this paper is that language models are increasingly asked to explain themselves before answering. A user, company, teacher, moderator, or search system may trust an answer more when the model writes a chain of intermediate thoughts, reviews its own answer, or lets several model voices argue before deciding. The hope is simple: more stated reasoning should expose mistakes and produce better decisions. This paper asks a different question: what if making the model say more also gives bias more room to enter? The setting is LLM alignment safety, where alignment means the model's behavior should stay close to human safety goals such as fairness and avoidance of stereotypes. The authors study prompt-based reasoning techniques, including Chain-of-Thought, Self-Reflection, and Multi-Agent Debating, across several models, fairness and stereotype tests, and languages. The paper serves anyone deploying reasoning-style language models who needs to know whether better reasoning scores can come with ethical risk.
252.wh: The hard part is that reasoning quality and safety are not the same measurement. A model can solve a puzzle more accurately after being asked to reason step by step, yet still produce answers that treat social groups unevenly or repeat stereotypes. The reason is that a reasoning prompt changes the path the model takes through language. It does not only ask for a final answer; it asks for intermediate explanations, checks, counterarguments, or debate turns. Each extra sentence can introduce associations learned from past text. Some associations help solve tasks, while others connect languages, identities, occupations, traits, or cultures in unfair ways. Fairness is also difficult to test because harm may appear differently across languages. A method that seems safer in English can still weaken alignment elsewhere. The paper therefore studies a tension: prompt designs meant to improve reasoning may also change the model's safety behavior in ways that average task success does not reveal.
252.naive: A smart beginner would try a direct rule: whenever a question is hard, ask the model to think step by step, check itself, or debate with other model instances. If the final answer improves, keep the prompting method. That fails because it treats the extra text as harmless scaffolding. In this paper's setting, the extra text is part of the behavior being tested. A self-review can rationalize a biased answer instead of correcting it. A debate can amplify a stereotype if several model voices draw from the same learned associations. A step-by-step explanation can make an unfair answer look more deliberate and therefore more trustworthy to a reader. Measuring only reasoning ability misses whether alignment has been weakened.
252.ap: The paper's central move is to audit reasoning prompts as safety interventions, not merely as reasoning aids. Instead of asking only whether Chain-of-Thought, Self-Reflection, and Multi-Agent Debating improve answers on reasoning tasks, the authors ask what happens to fairness and stereotype behavior when those prompts are used. The concrete comparison is between model behavior under different prompt-based reasoning styles and model behavior on fairness-oriented tests. The title captures the mechanism being suspected: the more the model is encouraged to say, the more surface area there is for unsafe associations to appear. The study spans multiple LLMs and multiple languages, which matters because the concern is not tied to one model release or one English-only test. The claim grounded in the abstract is not that reasoning prompts are useless. It is sharper: techniques that improve reasoning capabilities can undermine model alignment, so a deployment choice that looks like a pure accuracy improvement may quietly add fairness risk.
252.mech: The mechanism starts with a set of language models and a set of prompt styles. One style likely asks for an answer directly. Chain-of-Thought asks the model to produce intermediate reasoning before the final answer. Self-Reflection asks the model to inspect or revise its own earlier response. Multi-Agent Debating sets up several model-generated positions and asks them to interact before a conclusion is chosen. The paper then runs these model-and-prompt combinations on fairness and stereotype benchmarks, which are test collections designed to reveal whether a model treats groups, identities, or social categories unevenly. For each case, the input is a prompt containing the test item and the requested reasoning format. The model transforms that input into a response, often with more intermediate language than a direct answer would contain. The response is then scored by the benchmark's fairness or stereotype criteria. The comparison asks whether the reasoning format changes the safety outcome: does the model become more aligned with fairness goals, stay the same, or become worse? The abstract says the experiments show that Chain-of-Thought, Self-Reflection, and Multi-Agent Debating can all undermine alignment, and that this pattern holds across different languages. The output of the study is therefore a risk map for prompt-based reasoning styles, not a new reasoning method.
252.math: The mathematical idea is controlled comparison under uncertainty. Controlled comparison means changing one part of the setup, such as the prompt style, while keeping the model, test item, and scoring target organized enough that differences in outcomes can be meaningfully attributed to the prompt condition. The uncertainty is ethical and statistical: a single response does not prove a model is fair or unfair, so the authors need repeated test cases across benchmarks, models, and languages. A benchmark is a structured pile of examples with expected ways to score harmful patterns; it turns a broad social concern into many small measurable checks. The important score is not only whether the answer is correct, but whether the answer or its reasoning expresses stereotype-consistent behavior or violates alignment expectations. Multi-language evaluation adds another mathematical pressure: the same prompting method must be compared across separate language settings, where word meanings and social associations may differ. The tradeoff is reasoning performance versus fairness risk. Prompting creates a longer sequence of generated text, and each position in that sequence is another choice made from learned language patterns. More choices can help with logic, but they also create more opportunities for biased associations to steer the final answer or justify it.
252.dots: This paper connects three recurring conference ideas: language-model reasoning, fairness auditing, and trust in generated answers. It sits near LLM and agent papers because Chain-of-Thought, Self-Reflection, and Multi-Agent Debating are all ways of turning a model from a single answer machine into a process that appears to deliberate. It also belongs to the fairness and responsible-AI family, where the shared question is how automated systems reuse past language and behavior without turning historical imbalance into neutral-looking evidence. Finally, it touches misinformation and trust work because a longer explanation can make a response sound more warranted even when the underlying behavior is unsafe. Neighboring papers in the same batch study LLM knowledge editing, misinformation tools, causal feature selection, and federated recommendation; this paper's version of the shared problem is prompt-level intervention. Instead of changing training data or internal weights, it asks whether changing the conversation format itself can alter ethical behavior.
252.ww: The finding is plausible because prompt-based reasoning does not add an independent moral checker from outside the model. It asks the same learned system to produce more language, reconsider its own language, or simulate several voices from the same underlying source. If the model has learned biased associations from web-scale text, extra reasoning can give those associations more paths to appear. A direct answer may expose only the final choice. A chain of reasoning can expose stereotypes in premises. A self-reflection step can preserve the first biased answer and then decorate it with a plausible correction that does not actually remove the harm. A debate can sound diverse while still drawing every participant from similar model behavior. Testing several models and languages strengthens the practical lesson because it reduces the chance that the risk is only a quirk of one system or one English prompt. The method works as an audit because it treats reasoning formats as experimental conditions and asks whether safety scores move when the format changes.
252.po: The payoff is a warning that reasoning prompts need safety evaluation before deployment. The abstract says these techniques improve reasoning capabilities, but the experiments show that Chain-of-Thought, Self-Reflection, and Multi-Agent Debating can undermine alignment across different languages. That gives practitioners a concrete capability: they can stop treating longer reasoning as automatically safer or more trustworthy. A model card, product review, or research evaluation should report not only whether a reasoning framework improves task success, but also whether it changes fairness and stereotype behavior. The result is especially useful for multilingual systems, where English-only safety checks can miss harms that appear elsewhere.
252.limits: The abstract does not specify which models, languages, benchmarks, prompt templates, or scoring rules were used, so the strength of the claim depends on those details. Fairness and stereotype benchmarks are useful warning devices, but they cannot cover every culture, identity, task, or real deployment setting. The study shows that the named prompting frameworks can undermine alignment; it does not prove that every reasoning prompt always increases harm or that no prompt design can reduce it. It also does not show whether the unsafe behavior comes from the extra length, the particular instructions, the benchmark wording, or the model's prior training. Deployment still requires task-specific testing.

253.bp: A recommender is trying to remember what a person tends to like while also noticing when that person changes. In a shopping, media, or web service, the useful evidence is often private: clicks, purchases, skips, repeated interests, and recent shifts in behavior. Sending all of that to one central training store can violate the privacy boundary that user-centric systems are supposed to respect. Federated learning is the natural alternative: each user device or client keeps its own records and contributes learning signals instead of raw behavior. This paper serves the harder version of that problem. The user is not fixed over time, and users are not copies of one another. FCUCR asks how a private, client-side recommender can keep long-term preference memory, adapt as behavior evolves, and still borrow useful collaborative signal from similar users without replacing each person's own decision logic.
253.wh: The hard part is that recommendation needs both memory and change. If a local model pays too much attention to the newest behavior, it can forget older preferences that still matter, such as a long-standing taste that has only been quiet for a while. If it holds too tightly to the past, it misses a real shift in the user's current needs. Privacy makes the tension sharper because the service cannot simply gather every user's full timeline in one place and compare everyone directly. Federated learning keeps data local, but that means each client trains on a narrow, uneven view of the world. Some users have rich histories; others have sparse or unusual behavior. The abstract names two resulting failures: temporal forgetting, where older preference knowledge weakens during later updates, and weakened collaborative personalization, where clients fail to benefit enough from related users under heterogeneous local data.
253.naive: A smart beginner would train a separate recommendation model on each user's local history and periodically combine model updates through a federated server. That avoids raw-data centralization and seems to give each user personalization. It fails in two ways. First, ordinary local updating treats new behavior as the main teacher, so the model can overwrite earlier preference patterns instead of carrying them forward. Second, averaging or sharing generic updates does not know which other users are truly useful for this client. Users differ in history length, item exposure, and preference shape. If collaboration ignores that heterogeneity, it can import irrelevant signal from the crowd or miss informative signal from users whose preferences are genuinely similar.
253.ap: The core move is to make federated recommendation continual and selective. Continual means the client updates over time without treating each update as a blank restart. The paper introduces time-aware self-distillation: during local updates, the model is guided to retain useful historical preference knowledge instead of letting recent examples erase it. Self-distillation here means the model's earlier behavior acts like a quiet teacher for its later behavior, so old preference structure still has a voice. Selective means collaboration is not just a global blend of all clients. FCUCR transfers inter-user prototypes, or compact summaries of preference patterns from similar users, to enrich each client's representation. The important constraint is that this extra knowledge should help the client understand related tastes while preserving its individual decision logic rather than forcing all similar users into one shared profile.
253.mech: The input is a set of federated clients, each holding its own user behavior data over time. Each client performs local recommendation updates without exposing the raw sequence of interactions. During those updates, FCUCR adds a time-aware self-distillation signal. Mechanically, the client's current model is not judged only by how well it fits the newest local behavior; it is also nudged to stay compatible with preference information learned from earlier periods. That creates a local memory pressure: newer evidence can change the model, but it must not casually erase historical preference structure. The second mechanism handles collaboration. Instead of assuming that every client should receive the same shared update, the system forms or uses inter-user prototypes, compact pattern carriers that stand for preference knowledge from similar users. A target client can then enrich its own representation with prototypes from users whose preferences look related. The output is an updated recommendation model for each client that combines three sources: its own recent behavior, retained historical preference knowledge, and selected knowledge from similar users. The server-side role, as supported by the abstract, is to coordinate federated learning and prototype transfer without collecting raw personal behavior. The final recommendations are still user-centric because the transferred prototype knowledge is meant to support, not replace, each client's individual decision rule.
253.math: The first mathematical idea is learning from examples over time. A model has adjustable settings that turn user behavior into recommendation scores. Local training changes those settings to reduce wrong recommendations on the client's data. The danger is that the most recent examples can pull the settings away from older patterns. Self-distillation adds a second kind of comparison: the later model is compared with useful behavior of an earlier model, so learning becomes a balance between fitting new evidence and preserving old knowledge. The word time-aware matters because the balance should respect when preferences appeared, rather than treating history as one undated pile. The second idea is similarity-based sharing. A prototype is a compressed representative pattern: not a user's raw record, but a summary of preference structure that can be compared and transferred. The system is assuming that users with similar preference summaries can teach each other something, while users with unlike summaries may mislead each other. The third idea is constrained sharing under privacy. Federated learning asks what useful signal may cross the client boundary. Here the traded signal is model knowledge or prototypes, not raw interaction logs. The central tradeoff is personalization versus privacy, and another is adaptation versus memory: the model must change enough to follow evolving behavior but stay stable enough to remember long-term taste.
253.dots: This paper connects directly to the repo's recommender-systems family, where the common pressure is choosing a small useful set from a huge, changing pile using partial evidence about users and items. It also connects to the privacy-federated-security family, where the recurring question is what signal can safely cross a boundary. FCUCR sits exactly between those pressures: recommendations improve when users can learn from one another, but privacy constraints prevent the simple centralized comparison of all histories. It also neighbors long-sequence and dynamic recommendation papers in the batch, such as SparseCTR's concern with long-term user behaviors and changing temporal patterns. The shared idea is that old behavior and recent behavior should not be mixed blindly. In the broader conference map, the paper touches similarity, sequence reasoning, learning from examples, and constrained sharing. Its distinctive surface is federated continual recommendation: keep personal data local, keep memory over time, and share only selected summaries from similar users.
253.ww: The approach should improve over the naive federated recommender because it attacks the two places where the naive version loses information. Time-aware self-distillation gives the local model a way to remember. Without it, the model's adjustable settings may chase recent behavior and weaken older preference patterns even when those patterns are still useful. With it, an earlier model's learned preference structure remains part of the training signal, so the update is less likely to treat recency as the only truth. Inter-user prototype transfer helps with the opposite problem: a single client may not have enough local evidence to understand all of a user's interests. If another user has a similar preference pattern, their compact prototype can add useful context without copying raw behavior. The method works only if the similarity measure behind prototype transfer is meaningful. When it is, collaboration becomes targeted rather than crowd-averaged, and the client gains shared knowledge while keeping its own local decision logic.
253.po: The payoff is a recommender that is better suited to long-term personalization under privacy constraints. According to the abstract, FCUCR addresses temporal forgetting with time-aware self-distillation and improves collaborative personalization under heterogeneous user data through inter-user prototype transfer. The reported experiments on four public benchmarks show superior effectiveness, compatibility, and practical applicability, although the abstract does not give the detailed metric values here. In practical terms, the paper buys a way for federated recommenders to adapt to evolving user behavior without discarding long-term preferences and without requiring a central store of raw user histories.
253.limits: The method assumes that past model behavior contains preference knowledge worth preserving. If a user's old behavior was accidental, stale, or caused by limited exposure, distillation may preserve the wrong signal. It also assumes that similar-user prototypes identify genuinely related preferences; poor similarity estimates can transfer misleading crowd knowledge. The privacy claim depends on the summaries and federated signals not leaking sensitive behavior, which the abstract does not prove in detail. The experiments use four public benchmarks, so the abstract supports effectiveness there, not automatic success on every deployed platform, user population, privacy setting, or rapidly shifting item catalog.

254.bp: This entry is not a conventional research paper with a tested method. It is a workshop announcement for FL@FM-TheWebConf'26, a forum about bringing together two large pressures in web machine learning: foundation models and federated learning. A foundation model is a general-purpose model trained from broad data so it can be adapted to many later tasks. Federated learning is a way to train or adapt models while data stays with the device, organization, or web service that produced it. The ordinary-world problem is easy to see: web systems want the broad skill of large models, but the useful evidence often sits inside browsers, phones, companies, platforms, and communities that cannot simply dump private records into one central training pile. The workshop matters because this is not one solved algorithmic task. It is an emerging field where researchers and practitioners need to compare assumptions, risks, and promising directions before the community hardens around one design.
254.wh: The difficulty comes from a direct conflict between hunger for shared evidence and the need to keep control over that evidence. Foundation models become useful because they absorb many kinds of examples, but web data is scattered, sensitive, legally constrained, and shaped by different local habits. Federated learning keeps raw data local, yet it does not remove every hard problem. A shared model still needs some signal from each participant, and that signal can be uneven, costly to communicate, hard to combine, or potentially revealing. The input gives only a workshop description, so it does not claim a particular solution to these tensions. It does say the field is emerging, which is important: the challenge is partly technical and partly collective. Researchers must decide what should be shared, how large models should be adapted across many holders of data, how privacy should be checked, and what counts as success when the web setting keeps changing.
254.naive: A smart beginner might say: train one huge model centrally, then send copies to every web application. That fails whenever the needed data cannot be centralized or when local users and organizations need different behavior. Another beginner might reverse the plan: keep every model local and never share anything. That protects the most obvious boundary, but it wastes the shared structure that many web tasks have in common, such as repeated language patterns, browsing patterns, recommendation needs, or safety failures. A third simple idea is to average local updates and call the result private. The repo's privacy-federated family data warns why this is too simple: summaries and updates can still leak information, and different clients may not be comparable.
254.ap: The central move of the workshop is convening work at the intersection rather than treating foundation models and federated learning as separate topics. In concrete terms, the field asks whether a large, broadly trained model can be adapted through many local data holders without forcing those holders to reveal their raw records. The foundation model supplies reusable general skill; federated learning supplies a boundary around private or organizational data. The workshop's role is to make this pairing explicit and to give researchers and practitioners a place to test which combinations are promising. Because the abstract is an announcement, the contribution is not a new training recipe, theorem, or benchmark result. Its core idea is agenda-setting: identify the joint problem, gather the people working on it, and chart possible research trajectories for web systems that need both large-model capability and decentralized data control.
254.mech: The mechanism described by the abstract is a research-community mechanism, not an algorithm with experimental steps. The input is an emerging set of works about federated foundation models for the web. Those works are brought into a workshop at The Web Conference 2026. The workshop then functions as a structured meeting place: researchers and practitioners submit, present, discuss, compare assumptions, and turn scattered efforts into clearer research directions. Under the hood of the topic itself, the expected technical loop can be inferred only at a high level. A broadly trained model exists first, carrying general behavior learned from wide data. Local web participants then hold data that could make the model more useful for their setting, but that data should not be copied freely into one central store. Federated learning would let each participant compute some limited training signal locally, such as an update or adaptation, and share only that shaped signal. A coordinator or shared process would combine the signals so the model improves or adapts across participants. What comes out, if the field succeeds, is a model that benefits from many web contexts while leaving raw local records under local control. The abstract does not specify the exact messages, aggregation rule, privacy guarantee, model size, or evaluation design.
254.math: The mathematical ideas are those forced by the topic, not by a specific method in the announcement. The first is learning from examples: a model has adjustable settings, sees evidence, compares its behavior with desired behavior, and changes the settings to reduce mistakes. A foundation model is the large-scale version of this idea, where broad examples create a reusable starting point for many later tasks. The second idea is constrained sharing. Federated learning asks what useful signal may cross a boundary while raw data stays behind it. That turns privacy into a measurable tradeoff, not a slogan: share too little and the common model cannot learn; share too much and a participant's records may be inferred from updates or behavior. The third idea is aggregation, meaning many local signals must be combined into one shared direction without letting noisy, unusual, or harmful signals dominate. Optimization also sits underneath the topic: the system must define what counts as wrong, costly, revealing, or unfair, then search for model changes that improve that score. The fit is natural because web intelligence is distributed. The useful pattern is spread across holders of data, while the risk is concentrated in what any one holder might reveal.
254.dots: This workshop announcement connects directly to the repo's privacy, federated, and security family: the shared question is what can safely cross a boundary when useful data is held by many parties. It also connects to the learning concept, because foundation models are reusable learners that must adapt from examples rather than hand-written rules. A neighboring idea is information: every shared update or summary carries some information, and the central question is whether it carries the right kind. It should carry repeated pattern that improves a model, not private detail that lets someone reconstruct a record or identify a participant. The announcement also sits near recommendation, retrieval, language models, and web infrastructure, because those are common web settings where large models and decentralized data collide. Unlike a single paper, this entry does not solve one subproblem. It marks a meeting point where several conference threads can be organized around the same underlying pressure: large shared capability under local data control.
254.ww: The pairing works as a research direction because the two ingredients compensate for each other's obvious weakness. Foundation models have broad skill, but their usual story assumes large collections of training data and often central control. Federated learning respects local control, but by itself it can be limited if each client has too little data or if local models never benefit from a broad shared starting point. Put together, a foundation model can provide the common base, while federated learning can provide local adaptation without raw data transfer. The reason this is better than the naive approaches is that it separates reusable pattern from private source material. If many web participants share only carefully shaped training signals, the system can learn what repeats across them while reducing direct exposure of their records. The workshop format works for a different reason: early fields need comparison before standardization. Researchers must find where the tradeoffs actually are, which privacy assumptions are too weak, and which tasks justify the cost of federated adaptation.
254.po: The payoff claimed by the abstract is a forum, not a measured performance gain. The workshop gives researchers and practitioners a place to discuss promising work and chart possible trajectories for federated foundation models on the web. That buys coordination in an emerging area where isolated papers could otherwise use incompatible assumptions about privacy, model adaptation, communication, evaluation, or deployment. If the topic matures, the practical payoff would be web-scale machine learning systems that gain from large general models while respecting the fact that useful web data is distributed across users, devices, organizations, and platforms. The abstract does not report experiments, numbers, or deployed systems.
254.limits: The main limit is that the input is a workshop announcement with a very thin abstract. It supports only the existence and purpose of the forum, the intersection of foundation models and federated learning, and the claim that the area is emerging. It does not prove that any federated foundation-model method works, protects privacy, saves communication, or improves web applications. The usual assumptions of the area still have to be checked: local participants must provide useful signals, shared updates must not leak unacceptable detail, aggregation must handle unequal and possibly harmful clients, and evaluation must reflect real web deployment rather than only convenient test settings.
